personality_voice.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Voldemort as Tom Riddle (both as sixteen-year-old and as diary-memory) presents a highly controlled, calculating, self-assured personality with a cold charm he deploys strategically. He is patient — spending months cultivating Ginny, feeding on her fears, and waiting for the right moment to reveal himself. He is theatrical and grandiose: he savours the confrontation with Harry, draws it out, monologues about his own brilliance ('poor but brilliant, parentless but so brave'), and relishes revealing his anagram. He is deeply contemptuous — of Hagrid ('big, blundering Hagrid'), of Muggles and Muggle-borns, of his own Muggle father. He is obsessively self-referential: his name, his lineage, his superiority are constant preoccupations. He is cunning and manipulative: he framed Hagrid deliberately, charmed Dippet, and crafted the diary as a long-range weapon. He laughs a 'high, cold laugh that didn't suit him.' His speech is measured and pleasant in tone but menacing in content — 'The longer you talk, the longer you stay alive.' He is also capable of losing composure when directly challenged, particularly about Dumbledore: 'The smile had gone from Riddle's face, to be replaced by a very ugly look.' He hisses defensively. He is hungry — his eyes 'roved over the lightning scar... their expression grew hungrier' — consumed by obsessive curiosity about Harry's survival. He is intellectually arrogant, comparing himself to Harry at length, drawing the Slytherin parallels with visible relish.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film Tom Riddle (Chamber of Secrets) preserves the core personality architecture well. He is calm, theatrical, and controlling in the Chamber scene. He withholds Harry's wand with a smile, delivers the revelation of his identity with deliberate flair, monologues about Ginny and the diary. His contempt for Muggles and Muggle-borns is present ('filthy Muggle father's name'). His grandiosity is intact: he announces himself as future greatest sorcerer and laughs at Fawkes and the Sorting Hat. He is composed but reacts sharply when Harry invokes Dumbledore's name. His laugh ('giggling') appears, though the screenplay describes it as giggling rather than the book's 'high, cold laugh.' The film's Riddle is somewhat condensed in monologue — several of his longer, more self-revealing speeches in the book (the extended comparison of himself to Harry, the explicit statement about his orphan background, the full explanation of his patience with Ginny) are trimmed. The 'hungry eyes' texture and the drawn-out psychological game are slightly reduced but still present. His speech in the film retains pleasant menace: 'I'm afraid I can't do that, Harry' and 'If you have any final words, Potter, you'd best speak them now.' The memory-of-Dippet scene from the book (showing young Riddle's nervousness, his reddening, his careful calculation in the headmaster's office) does not appear in the film corpus; instead the film cuts directly to the dungeon confrontation with Hagrid. This removes some texture of Riddle's social performance and controlled vulnerability before authority figures.
personality_voice.difference: The film preserves the dominant traits: cold charm, grandiosity, contempt, theatrical self-revelation, obsessive curiosity about Harry. Minor losses: (1) the Dippet office scene — showing Riddle's calculated social performance (nervous exterior, careful dissembling, biting his lip in thought) — is absent from the film, removing one dimension of his manipulative persona. (2) The extended self-comparison to Harry ('Both half-bloods, orphans, raised by Muggles... probably the only two Parselmouths') is condensed to the anagram reveal and a briefer version, losing some of the obsessive mirroring quality. (3) The book's specific laugh description ('a high, cold laugh that didn't suit him') is rendered as giggling in the screenplay, a minor tonal difference. (4) The book has Riddle explicitly acknowledge Dumbledore's surveillance with studied carelessness ('annoyingly close watch'), showing controlled contempt for even those who see through him; the film compresses this. These are secondary traits; the main personality profile is intact.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: A minor penalty is warranted. The dominant personality — cold charm, grandiosity, manipulation, contempt, theatrical self-disclosure — is directly evidenced in the film corpus and is faithful. The losses are real but secondary: the Dippet scene texture, the extended self-mirroring speech, the precise laugh quality. None of these fundamentally change who Riddle is, but their combined absence slightly flattens the psychological portrait. Score falls in the 18–22 band, toward the higher end given strong preservation of the main traits.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Tom Riddle/Voldemort functions as: (1) the primary antagonist of the Chamber storyline, operating through the diary as a long-range instrument; (2) the architect of the entire year's events — he manipulated Ginny, directed the attacks, and engineered the situation to draw Harry into the Chamber; (3) the revealer of key plot information (Ginny's role, his own identity, the anagram, the mechanism of the diary); (4) the active agent of Harry's near-death (commanding the basilisk, taunting Harry as he dies); (5) the vehicle for the series' central thematic revelation — that he is Voldemort, that he transferred powers to Harry, that choices matter more than abilities. His agency is total within the Chamber: he holds the wand, calls the basilisk, controls Ginny's fate, drives every beat of the confrontation. He also has earlier narrative agency as the diary-memory interacting with Harry through writing, as the young Riddle exposing Hagrid. Outside the Chamber, he functions as a looming presence referenced by many characters (Dobby, the Weasleys, Lucius, Dumbledore), establishing his shadow over the wizarding world.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves most of this agency. Riddle controls the Chamber confrontation, holds Harry's wand, reveals his identity, calls the basilisk, and taunts the dying Harry. He engineers Ginny's possession and the attacks. The diary-writing scene (though compressed — Ron's memory of the trophy is excluded per the non-theatrical rule, making Hermione the one who drives the theory about the diary being significant) is present. The film's Riddle is the architect of events and the revealer of plot information. His agency in the Chamber is intact. The one notable structural shift: the film omits the Dippet memory sequence, which in the book gives Riddle a scene of active, calculating agency — choosing to wait, deciding to follow Hagrid, thinking through his options — entirely driven by Riddle's initiative. In the film, the memory jumps straight to Riddle confronting Hagrid, cutting the process of his decision-making. The book also has Riddle's extended 'I framed Hagrid deliberately' speech with more explicit acknowledgment of his manipulation of Dippet ('poor but brilliant... on the other hand, big, blundering Hagrid'), which the film compresses but retains the core.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The main loss is the Dippet office scene: in the book, Riddle has a complete scene of agency — he is the one who decides to act, who makes the calculation, who follows Hagrid and exposes him. The film collapses this to showing only the Hagrid confrontation, removing the preceding decision sequence. This is a modest agency loss. The rest of his narrative function is preserved: he is the antagonist, the architect, the revealer, the threat in the Chamber.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The role and agency are substantially preserved. The Dippet scene removal reduces one beat of shown agency, but Riddle's overall narrative function — controlling the Chamber confrontation, directing events, being the primary threat — is fully present. Score in the 14–17 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Book Riddle's motivations in this corpus are: (1) survival and power — the diary was created specifically to survive beyond Hogwarts and eventually return as Voldemort; (2) obsessive hatred of his Muggle father and rejection of his Muggle identity — 'You think I was going to use my filthy Muggle father's name forever? I, in whose veins runs the blood of Salazar Slytherin'; (3) consuming need to understand how Harry survived — 'There was an odd red gleam in his hungry eyes'; (4) desire to finish Slytherin's 'noble work' (purging Muggle-borns); (5) a specific, focused resentment of his orphan past and Muggle orphanage — 'Id much rather stay at Hogwarts than go back to that —'; (6) the need to be acknowledged as the greatest. The internal conflict is limited but present: the book shows young Riddle calculating and uncertain in Dippet's office — he lies ('No, sir') but Harry recognises it as the same kind of lie he himself has told, a lie driven by need. This moment of comparable insecurity (needing Hogwarts, not wanting to return to the orphanage) is a genuine motivational complexity — it connects Riddle's horror of his origins to his actions.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves: hatred of his Muggle father and name, the aspiration to be the greatest sorcerer, the desire to finish Slytherin's work, the need to understand Harry's survival. These are all explicitly stated in the Chamber scene. The motivation of the diary as a survival mechanism is explained ('I decided to leave behind a diary, preserving my sixteen-year-old self'). What is largely lost: the Dippet scene and the line 'I'd much rather stay at Hogwarts than go back to that —' which directly establishes the orphanage-horror as a motivating force. This is the most textured motivational beat in the corpus — it shows Riddle's vulnerability and the human root of his monstrousness. Without it, his motivation becomes more purely ideological (Slytherin's heir, anti-Muggle) and less psychologically grounded in personal trauma and desperate need.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivations (power, identity, hatred of Muggle heritage, survival, obsession with Harry) are present in the film. The loss is the orphanage motivation — the specific fear of return to a Muggle world he despises, which humanises and complicates his ideology. The film's Riddle is motivated by ideology and power but lacks the shown personal desperation that roots those motivations in something more vulnerable.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but not wrong. The ideological and power-hunger motivations are intact. The personal/traumatic root is absent due to the Dippet scene cut, making the motivations slightly flatter. Score in the 11–13 range.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for present material; reasonably inferred for the loss

character_arc.book_baseline: Within this specific book (Chamber of Secrets), Voldemort does not have a traditional developmental arc — he is the antagonist operating through a past self. The 'arc' is structural: (1) Riddle as historical figure — a brilliant, troubled orphan who chose darkness; (2) Riddle as diary-memory — a sixteen-year-old self preserved to eventually complete Slytherin's work; (3) Riddle's revelation as Voldemort — the anagram, the identity reveal, connecting the boy to the Dark Lord; (4) Riddle's near-return — growing solid as Ginny weakens, almost achieving re-embodiment; (5) Riddle's destruction — the diary pierced, the memory obliterated. The important arc-step is the Dippet scene: it shows the young Riddle before full corruption — nervous, calculating, still capable of social performance, still tethered to Hogwarts by need. This is the last glimpse of the human before the monster, and it gives the Chamber sequence its retroactive weight. Dumbledore's later commentary ('the clever, handsome boy who was once Head Boy here') confirms this arc of transformation from brilliant student to Dark Lord.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the structural arc: past brilliant student → diary-memory → identity reveal → near-return → destruction. Dumbledore's office scene includes his commentary on Riddle's brilliance and transformation. The anagram reveal is present and effective. The near-return (Riddle growing more solid) is shown. The diary's destruction ends his presence. What is missing: the Dippet scene, which is the only in-film depiction of young Riddle as still-human and vulnerable, showing the step between brilliant student and monster. Without it, the film's version of the arc lacks the before-corruption moment, jumping straight to the manipulative confrontation with Hagrid.
character_arc.difference: The Dippet scene is the key arc-step missing. It establishes that Riddle was not always the cold manipulator — he needed things, feared being sent back to the orphanage, was observed with suspicion by Dumbledore. The film compresses this to just the Hagrid confrontation (already showing him in full manipulative mode) and Dumbledore's retrospective commentary. The arc is present but one of its human-origin steps is cut.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but the major beats survive. The missing Dippet step means the before/after transition is less visible — the arc goes from 'award-winning student' (heard about, not seen) to 'cold manipulator' without the intermediate 'desperate, calculating boy' step. This is a noticeable compression. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The corpus presents three key relationships for Riddle/Voldemort: (1) Riddle and Harry — the core dynamic is one of obsessive mirroring and rivalry. Riddle is fascinated by Harry, studies him, draws parallels ('Both half-bloods, orphans, raised by Muggles... we even look something alike'), and is genuinely hungry to understand him. The power dynamic shifts — Riddle holds all the cards initially, but Harry's defiance and Dumbledore's loyalty reverse it. The relationship is defined by Riddle's need to understand, explain, and ultimately destroy Harry, and by Harry's refusal to be intimidated despite being outmatched. (2) Riddle and Dumbledore — adversarial, but Dumbledore is the one person Riddle cannot dismiss. Book Riddle acknowledges being watched ('kept an annoyingly close watch'), shows defensive reaction to Harry's invocation of Dumbledore's name (hissing, loss of composure), and is clearly rattled by Dumbledore's continued influence even from a distance. The relationship is characterised by Riddle's barely-contained fear-masked-as-contempt. (3) Riddle and Hagrid — exploitative and contemptuous. Riddle used Hagrid as a convenient scapegoat ('It was my word against Hagrid's'), showing his willingness to destroy someone weaker without remorse. (4) Riddle and Ginny — purely instrumental. Ginny is a vessel, a tool, described with cold disdain ('silly little brat,' 'pitiful worries and woes').
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry–Riddle dynamic is well-preserved: the mirroring fascination, the power imbalance, Harry's defiance, Riddle's obsessive curiosity about Harry's survival. The anagram reveal and the Chamber confrontation maintain this dynamic effectively. The Dumbledore dynamic is preserved in outline — Riddle reacts to Harry's invocation of Dumbledore, the 'mere memory of me' line is present — but the book's more specific acknowledgment of Dumbledore's persistent surveillance ('annoyingly close watch') is absent, making Riddle's fear of Dumbledore slightly less textured. The Hagrid relationship is preserved in the memory scene, though the full contemptuous comparison ('poor but brilliant... on the other hand, big, blundering Hagrid') is condensed. The Ginny relationship is preserved instrumentally. The book's extended self-comparison to Harry ('Strange likenesses between us... we even look something alike') is substantially cut, reducing the mirroring quality of the Harry relationship.
key_relationships.difference: The main loss is in the Harry relationship: the book's extended mirroring speech is significantly compressed in the film, reducing the obsessive quality of Riddle's fascination with their parallels. The Dumbledore dynamic is slightly less specific. Otherwise the key relationships are recognisable and functional.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly faithful in function and dynamic, but the Harry relationship loses some of its mirroring texture (the extended comparison is compressed), and the Dumbledore fear-dynamic is slightly less specific. Score in the 7–8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book corpus establishes several layers of complexity for Riddle/Voldemort: (1) The orphan-background vulnerability — his reddening at 'Muggle orphanage,' his desperate 'I'd much rather stay at Hogwarts than go back to that —', which shows a human wound beneath the ideology; (2) The social chameleon quality — in Dippet's office, he is nervous, polite, careful; in the dungeon, he is sharp and commanding; with Harry in the Chamber, he is pleasant-menacing; (3) The obsessive self-mirroring with Harry — he genuinely finds Harry fascinating not just as a puzzle but as a distorted reflection, spending considerable effort drawing the parallels; (4) The calculated patience — 'I've always been able to charm the people I needed'; months of patient manipulation of Ginny; years of planning via the diary; (5) The ideological contradiction — he despises Muggles and Muggle-borns, yet he himself is half-Muggle, a contradiction he resolves through grandiose self-exception ('I, in whose veins runs the blood of Salazar Slytherin'); (6) His intellectual vanity — framing himself as the most brilliant Hogwarts student, the greatest sorcerer, while being genuinely fascinated by what he cannot explain (Harry's survival); (7) The cold laugh 'that didn't suit him' — a detail suggesting the persona is partly constructed, that the Dark Lord voice is a performance layered over the boy.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves: calculated patience, contempt for Muggles, the half-blood contradiction (stated explicitly), intellectual vanity, the taunting of dying Harry. It loses: the full Dippet scene (orphan vulnerability, social performance before authority), the extended self-mirroring speech with Harry, the nuanced description of his laughter as mismatched to him, and the specific detail of Riddle biting his lip and thinking after leaving Dippet's office. The film's Riddle is complex within the Chamber scene but lacks the before-Chamber material that shows him in a different register — uncertain, performing vulnerability, calculating under pressure from authority. This is the richest source of his psychological complexity in the corpus, and its absence makes the film's Riddle more uniformly cold and in-control.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The main complexity loss is the Dippet scene and its associated material: the orphan vulnerability, the social performance, the moment of visible calculation before acting. The mirroring-with-Harry is compressed. The result is a Riddle who is complex within a single register (cool menace) but lacks the layering of registers that the book provides.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification. The film Riddle is not flattened to a single trait, but the most textured source of his psychological complexity (the Dippet scene) is absent, and the mirroring with Harry is compressed. The ideological contradiction (half-blood who despises Muggles) survives but the personal-wound dimension that gives it force is largely gone. Score in the 8–10 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; directly evidenced for what is absent

Riddle's extended self-mirroring speech to Harry ('Both half-bloods, orphans, raised by Muggles... we even look something alike... but after all, it was merely a lucky chance') — substantially cut in the film, reducing the obsessive parallel-drawing

Riddle's explicit contemptuous comparison of himself to Hagrid in the memory scene ('poor but brilliant, parentless but so brave... on the other hand, big, blundering Hagrid') — compressed in the film
The specific description of Riddle's laugh as 'a high, cold laugh that didn't suit him' — rendered as giggling in the screenplay, a minor tonal loss

The line 'I'd much rather stay at Hogwarts than go back to that —' — the orphanage-horror motivation — absent from the film due to the Dippet scene cut

score_caps_applied: No hard cap applied. Total of 78 is below the 80-cap threshold (key relationships are altered but not substantially changed). The 85-cap is the relevant ceiling: complexity and nuance losses are real but the remaining material is substantially faithful, placing the score appropriately in the upper-70s range without triggering the cap mechanically.
key_observations: The film's portrayal of Tom Riddle/Voldemort in Chamber of Secrets is substantially faithful in its most visible dimensions: the cold charm, grandiosity, contempt, theatrical self-disclosure, and agency in the Chamber confrontation are all well-preserved. The primary adaptation loss is the Dippet office scene — the one moment in the corpus where Riddle is shown as a calculating but still-vulnerable human, performing social deference while concealing his true intent, driven by the desperate need not to return to a Muggle orphanage. This scene's absence removes the most psychologically layered material in the corpus: the orphan wound, the social chameleon quality, the visible decision-making, and the last glimpse of the boy before the monster. Its loss modestly flattens the motivational complexity and one key arc-step. Secondary losses — the compressed self-mirroring speech with Harry, the trimmed Dumbledore-fear texture — are real but minor. The film's Riddle is recognisably the same character operating in the same way, but with less psychological depth beneath the menace.
